en.title: Educational Management: the whole course
en.short: What educational management covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Educational management is the study of how schools, colleges and other learning institutions are planned, organised, led, financed and improved. It draws on management, economics, law, psychology and sociology, but its test is educational: does a decision help teaching and learning? It prepares people for roles such as head teacher, principal, school administrator, planning officer, inspector, quality assurance officer and ministry official. The field is not only about running an institution smoothly. It asks who gets access, how resources are shared, how teachers are supported and how results are checked. Because education is public and political, managers must explain decisions to parents, staff, government and the community.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Programmes differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, educational management is usually studied within a Bachelor of Education or a Bachelor of Arts or Science in Education, often over four years. Master of Education programmes commonly take one to two years, and a doctorate takes longer. The National Universities Commission regulates university programmes, and the National Commission for Colleges of Education regulates colleges of education. Check your own handbook for the exact award, duration and course requirements.

In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree commonly takes three years and a master’s one year. In the United States, a bachelor’s commonly takes four years. Some institutions offer educational management as a major; others require a first degree or teaching qualification. Accreditation and entry requirements vary. Confirm current rules with your department and the relevant regulator.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage defines the field and its setting. You study what educational management is, then education systems and structures, management functions, and the main schools of management thought. Organisational behaviour and the school as an organisation show how people and roles work together. Basics of educational planning, an introduction to the economics of education, and educational statistics and data give you planning and evidence tools.

The core stage applies these ideas. Leadership theories come first, followed by school administration and management. Human resource management covers staff recruitment, development and appraisal. Finance and budgeting, school plant and facilities, curriculum and instructional management, supervision and inspection, and quality assurance deal with resources and teaching. Policy and reform, law and school governance, records and information management, change and innovation, and school and community relations widen the manager’s view. Comparative and international education management, ethics and professionalism, and research methods complete the core.

At master’s level, advanced theories, strategic management, advanced research methods and dissertation work deepen the same themes. Digital transformation and data-driven management are now often included. The order can vary, but the sequence moves from concepts to practice, evidence and strategy.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read each topic with a question in mind: what problem does this idea help a school solve? Keep a glossary of terms such as management, administration, leadership, supervision and governance. These words are often used loosely, so learn the difference.

Use cases from a school you know, but change names and avoid private details. For finance and statistics, practise simple calculations and check every figure. For law and policy, name the country and check the current official source, because rules change. Write short summaries of each theory: its main claim, its author or school, and one criticism.

For research methods, learn to judge a sample, a questionnaire and a claim. At master’s level, read journal articles and keep a record of sources. Form a study group for discussion, but write your own answers.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is to treat management as business management with children added. Schools have goals, values and public accountability that differ from a company. Another is to learn lists of functions without seeing how they connect in a real school.

Students often quote a theory without naming its limits or the country where it was developed. Some confuse administration with leadership, or supervision with inspection. In finance, they copy figures without showing the calculation. In law, they state a Nigerian or British rule as if it were universal.

In research, a frequent fault is a conclusion that goes beyond the data. A questionnaire given to one class cannot describe a whole country. Another fault is ignoring ethics: consent, privacy and honest reporting of results. Check your work for these errors before you submit it.

keyPoints: Educational management applies management ideas to schools, colleges and education systems.
Degree length, title and accreditation differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Study the sequence from concepts and systems to administration, finance, law, quality and research.
Use real school cases and current official rules when you apply theory.
Educational decisions should be judged by whether they support teaching and learning.
At master’s level, theory, strategy and research methods become more demanding.

en.title: What Is Educational Management?
en.short: Definitions, scope at classroom, school and system levels, and management, administration and leadership.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.text:
Educational management is the process of planning, organising, coordinating and controlling resources and people to achieve educational goals. Educational administration is often used for the same work, but usage varies. In some traditions administration means the higher-level running of an education system, while management means work inside institutions; in others the words are interchangeable. Check how your own country or course uses them.

Leadership is different again. Leadership is influence that sets direction, builds commitment and guides change. Management is more about order, systems and resources. A head can manage well but lead poorly, or lead with weak routines. Effective schools need both.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text:
At classroom level, the teacher manages the learning environment: time, seating, routines, materials, behaviour and assessment. At school level, the head teacher or principal manages staff, curriculum delivery, finance, records, facilities and relations with parents. At system level, officials in ministries, districts or agencies manage policy, standards, funding, teacher supply and monitoring across many schools.

The levels connect. A system rule on class size reaches the classroom through the school timetable. A classroom problem, such as repeated lateness, may need a school policy and system support.

sections.heading: Roles and importance
sections.text:
Educational managers include heads of department, school heads, supervisors and education officers. Their roles are to set goals, allocate resources, coordinate staff, maintain records, support teaching and report to parents and authorities. They also protect fairness and safety.

Their importance lies in creating conditions where teaching and learning can happen. A manager who plans the timetable, checks attendance and listens to teachers helps the school run calmly. A manager who ignores these tasks leaves teachers to cope alone.

Case: In a secondary school in Kumasi, the head notices that Form One results are weak. She checks the timetable and finds science lessons clash with sports. She meets the science teachers, adjusts the timetable and agrees a simple record of missed lessons. The change shows management linking classroom problems to school organisation.

keyPoints: Educational management is planning, organising, coordinating and controlling resources to achieve educational goals.
Educational administration is often used interchangeably with management, but some traditions reserve it for higher-level system work.
Leadership is influence that sets direction and guides change; management stresses order, systems and resources.
The scope runs from classroom routines through school coordination to system policy and monitoring.
Educational managers include department heads, school heads, supervisors and education officers.
Good management creates orderly, fair conditions that support teaching and learning.

en.title: Education Systems and Structures
en.short: Formal education levels, school types, and the ministries, boards and agencies that govern them.

sections.heading: Formal levels
sections.text: Formal education is planned learning in schools, colleges and universities that leads to recognised certificates. UNESCO’s International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) groups levels so countries can be compared, but ages, durations and names vary. Early childhood education comes before primary school and may be called nursery, kindergarten or pre-primary. Primary education is usually the first compulsory stage. Secondary education follows primary and is often split into junior and senior cycles. Tertiary education includes universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, offering degrees, diplomas and certificates.

sections.heading: School types
sections.text: Schools differ by purpose and owner. Academic secondary schools prepare students for examinations and further study. Technical and vocational education and training (TVET) teaches practical skills for trades, crafts and occupations; it may be at secondary or post-secondary level and can include apprenticeships. Special schools support learners with disabilities, while many systems also promote inclusive education in ordinary schools. Schools may be public, private, faith-based or community-run. Leaving certificates and entry rules are set nationally or by examining bodies, so they differ by country.

sections.heading: Governance roles
sections.text: A ministry of education is a government department that sets policy and manages public funding. Boards are committees with defined powers, such as examinations, teacher employment or school management. Agencies are public bodies that deliver services, such as curriculum development, quality assurance or examinations. School governance bodies, such as boards of management or school-based management committees, oversee individual schools and link them to parents and the community. Some systems are centralised; others share power with states, counties or districts. Case: in Nigeria, the Federal Ministry of Education sets national policy, state ministries run state schools, the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) supports basic education, and School-Based Management Committees (SBMCs) take part in school governance. In Kenya, the Ministry of Education sets policy, the Teachers Service Commission employs public-school teachers, and boards of management govern public schools. These arrangements are country-specific.

keyPoints: Formal education runs from early childhood and primary through secondary to tertiary, with names and durations varying by country.
Technical and vocational education and training (TVET) teaches practical skills and may sit at secondary or post-secondary level.
Ministries set education policy and public funding, while boards and agencies carry out defined functions.
School governance bodies oversee individual schools and connect them with parents and communities.
Governance can be centralised or shared with states, counties or districts.
Nigeria and Kenya show country-specific arrangements, so always check the current national system.

en.title: Management Functions in Schools and Colleges
en.short: The six management functions and how schools use them to reach educational goals.

sections.heading: Six functions
sections.text: Management functions are the main tasks managers perform to turn resources into results. In education the common set is planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating and controlling. They overlap and repeat in a cycle; a principal may plan a new timetable, organise rooms, staff teachers, direct a briefing, coordinate departments and control the result. Writers group them differently, so treat the list as a practical map, not a fixed law.

sections.heading: Planning and organising
sections.text: Planning sets goals and decides in advance what to do, who will do it, when and with what resources. A college planning a new evening programme first states its aim, estimates student numbers, costs and staff needs, and sets dates. Organising arranges people and materials into a workable structure: departments, committees, timetables, classrooms and lines of responsibility. A clear structure shows who reports to whom and prevents two people from claiming the same task.

sections.heading: Staffing and directing
sections.text: Staffing means getting the right people into the right posts: recruitment, selection, appointment, induction, development and retention. A school may advertise a science post, check qualifications, interview candidates and give a new teacher a mentor. Directing, also called leading or supervising, guides staff day to day through instructions, meetings, motivation and support. It links people to the plan, so a head teacher explains a reading target and helps teachers use it.

sections.heading: Coordinating and controlling
sections.text: Coordinating harmonises separate efforts so they support one goal. In a secondary school in Ibadan, Mrs Adeyemi, an invented principal, coordinates the timetable, examinations office and heads of department before a new term. Controlling compares performance with the plan and corrects gaps. It uses records, observation, test results and meetings. If attendance falls, the school checks causes, adjusts actions and reviews again. The functions work together: planning without staffing or control remains paper.

keyPoints: Planning sets goals and decides actions, timing and resources in advance.
Organising arranges people, tasks and resources into a clear structure.
Staffing covers recruitment, selection, induction and development of staff.
Directing guides and motivates staff day to day, while coordinating harmonises their efforts.
Controlling compares results with plans and corrects gaps.
The functions overlap and work as a cycle to achieve educational goals.

en.title: Management Thought and Schools
en.short: Classical, bureaucratic, human relations, systems and contingency approaches, with school examples.

sections.heading: Classical and bureaucratic
sections.text: Classical management looks for efficiency through clear tasks, rules and control. Scientific management (Taylor) studied work methods and timing; administrative management (Fayol) proposed principles such as unity of command, division of labour and a clear chain of authority. Bureaucracy, described by Weber as an ideal type, adds hierarchy, written rules, records, impersonal treatment and appointment by merit. In schools these ideas appear in timetables, job descriptions, admission rules and record keeping. Strength: order, consistency and accountability. Limit: they can treat teachers as machine parts, ignore professional judgement and informal relationships, and produce slow, rule-bound administration.

sections.heading: Human relations
sections.text: The human relations approach grew from Elton Mayo’s Hawthorne studies. It holds that workers have social and emotional needs, and that morale, informal groups and participation affect output. In a school, this means listening to staff, involving teachers in decisions and recognising teamwork. Strength: it can improve commitment and cooperation. Limit: good feelings alone do not guarantee learning; the approach can underplay structure, pay, conflict and external pressure, and participation can become token.

sections.heading: Systems and contingency
sections.text: Systems thinking sees a school as an open system of interdependent parts: inputs (students, staff, funds), processes (teaching, administration), outputs (learning, results) and feedback from parents and examinations, all shaped by the environment. Strength: it encourages planning and shows that a problem in one part affects others. Limit: outputs are hard to measure and power struggles may be missed. Contingency theory says there is no one best way; management should fit the situation, such as school size, resources, staff skill and the pace of change. Strength: flexible and realistic. Limit: it can become an excuse for ad hoc decisions.

sections.heading: Case in practice
sections.text: At a large Kenyan college, the principal uses written rules and a fixed timetable for fairness (classical and bureaucratic). She holds department meetings so teachers shape decisions (human relations), tracks enrolment and results as a system, and adapts when a new curriculum or staff shortage appears (contingency). Effective managers combine approaches.

keyPoints: Classical management seeks efficiency through clear tasks, rules and control.
Bureaucracy adds hierarchy, written rules, records and merit appointment.
Human relations stresses morale, informal groups and participation.
Systems theory sees the school as interdependent parts shaped by its environment.
Contingency theory says management should fit the situation; there is no one best way.
Each approach has strengths and limits, so school leaders usually combine them.

en.title: Organisational Behaviour in Schools
en.short: How individuals and groups behave in schools, and how managers shape motivation, communication, conflict and climate.

sections.heading: Individuals and motivation
sections.text: Organisational behaviour is the study of how people act in organisations. Individual behaviour is shaped by needs, beliefs, skills and working conditions. Motivation is the force that starts and sustains effort. Two ideas: Maslow’s hierarchy suggests people act on lower needs such as safety before higher ones; Herzberg’s two-factor theory separates hygiene factors (pay, conditions) from motivators (achievement, recognition). Managers should treat these as guides. Fair influence means listening, explaining decisions, and applying rules consistently.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.text: Communication is the exchange of meaning. A simple model has a sender, a message, a channel, a receiver and feedback. Noise is anything that distorts it, such as unclear language or a busy staffroom. Staff meetings, notice boards, parents’ messages and one-to-one talks all carry meaning. Managers should choose the channel to suit the message, check understanding, and make space for questions. Listening is part of communication, not a pause before speaking.

sections.heading: Groups and conflict
sections.text: Group dynamics is how groups form and influence members. A group is two or more people who interact and depend on one another. Group norms are shared rules of behaviour; roles are the parts people play. Groups can support learning through teamwork, but they can also exclude people or pressure members to conform. Conflict is disagreement between people or groups. It can be healthy when it tests ideas, but harmful when it becomes personal. Managers should address conflict early, separate the people from the problem, hear both sides, and agree a way forward.

sections.heading: School climate
sections.text: School climate is the shared perception of how a school feels: its safety, relationships, fairness and expectations. A positive climate supports teaching and learning; a poor one raises staff turnover. Example: a new principal in a Nigerian secondary school who found that staff meetings were used only for announcements could add short problem-solving sessions and a fair duty roster, so that teachers feel heard. Managers influence behaviour through example, fair rules, recognition and clear communication.

keyPoints: Organisational behaviour studies how individuals and groups act in a school.
Motivation starts and sustains effort, and both working conditions and recognition affect it.
Communication needs a clear message, a suitable channel and feedback, and listening is part of it.
Group dynamics is how groups form and influence members; norms and roles shape behaviour.
Conflict can be healthy when it tests ideas, but managers should address it early and fairly.
School climate is the shared perception of safety, relationships, fairness and expectations, and managers shape it by example and consistent rules.

en.title: The School as an Organization
en.short: School goals, formal and informal structure, culture, roles, open systems and environments.

sections.heading: Goals and structure
sections.text:
A school is an organization: a group of people working together with rules and resources to reach shared purposes. Its goals are the outcomes it intends, such as learning, safety and preparation for further study or work. Some goals are official, written in plans; others are informal and held by staff or parents.

Formal structure is the official arrangement of positions, committees, rules and timetable. It shows who reports to whom. Informal structure is the network of friendships, advice and influence that grows alongside it. Both affect how work is done.

sections.heading: Culture and roles
sections.text:
Culture is the shared beliefs, values, customs and symbols that shape behaviour. A school may value punctuality, respect or competition; these show in assemblies, notices and how staff speak to students. Culture can support change or resist it.

A role is the set of expected behaviours attached to a position. The head teacher, class teacher, bursar, counsellor and student prefect each have roles. Role conflict occurs when expectations clash, for example when a teacher is also a parent in the same school.

sections.heading: Open systems
sections.text:
A school is an open system: it takes inputs from outside, such as students, staff, money and policy; transforms them through teaching and learning; and sends outputs, such as results and graduates, back to society. Feedback from parents, employers and inspectors then adjusts the system.

The internal environment includes staff, students, facilities, culture and available time. The external environment includes government rules, the local community, the economy and technology. Managers must read both. A new national curriculum rule, for example, may require timetable and training decisions inside the school.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider a secondary school in Kumasi, Ghana. The head, Mr Mensah, learns that a new government policy requires more mathematics lessons. He checks the timetable, asks teachers for views, and meets parents. The formal structure carries the change; informal networks and culture affect how smoothly it runs.

keyPoints: A school is an organization with official goals and informal goals held by people.
Formal structure is the official hierarchy, rules and timetable; informal structure is the network of relationships.
Culture is the shared beliefs, values and customs that shape behaviour.
Roles are expected behaviours attached to positions, and role conflict occurs when expectations clash.
A school is an open system that takes inputs, transforms them and produces outputs with feedback.
Internal and external environments both shape school life and management decisions.

en.title: Basics of Educational Planning
en.short: Meaning and rationale of educational planning, strategic and operational plans, steps, data and challenges.

sections.heading: Meaning and rationale
sections.text:
Educational planning is the process of deciding in advance what education should achieve, how it will be done, who will do it, and what resources are needed. It links aims to action.

Its rationale is that resources such as teachers, classrooms, money and time are limited. Planning helps a school or system use them wisely, coordinate activities, reduce uncertainty, and check goals. It supports fairness by directing resources to greater need.

sections.heading: Strategic and operational
sections.text:
A strategic plan sets broad, longer-term direction for a whole school or system: vision, priorities and major targets. It usually covers several years, though periods vary. An operational plan turns strategy into shorter-term action, often for a year or term. It names specific tasks, responsibilities, timelines, budgets and success measures.

Example: a strategic plan may aim to improve science results; the operational plan may schedule laboratory repairs, teacher training and monthly progress checks.

sections.heading: Steps and data
sections.text:
Steps are: assess needs and the current situation; set clear goals and measurable objectives; consider options and choose the best; prepare an action plan with tasks, people, time and resources; implement; monitor and evaluate; then revise.

Data needs include enrolment and attendance, population trends, teacher numbers and qualifications, classrooms and facilities, finance, learning outcomes, and community needs. Use reliable, recent, cross-checked data.

sections.heading: Challenges and goals
sections.text:
Common challenges include unreliable data, limited funds, rapid enrolment growth, staff shortages, weak implementation and poor monitoring. Plans also fail when staff are not involved or targets are unrealistic.

To link planning to goals, start from the school’s or system’s stated aims, such as access, equity, quality and relevance. Set school-level targets and resource decisions that serve those aims, and align them with current official ministry or district guidelines. A school expecting 120 new students and using its own standard of 40 per class needs at least 120 ÷ 40 = 3 extra classes. It should plan classrooms, teachers and timetables.

keyPoints: Educational planning decides in advance what education should achieve, how it will be done and what resources are needed.
Planning is needed because resources are limited and activities must be coordinated, fair and checked.
A strategic plan gives longer-term direction, while an operational plan sets shorter-term tasks, responsibilities and budgets.
The planning cycle runs from needs assessment and goal setting to action, implementation, monitoring and revision.
Planners need reliable data on enrolment, teachers, facilities, finance and learning outcomes.
A simple capacity check is extra classes = expected new students ÷ class-size standard, rounded up.

en.title: Introduction to the Economics of Education
en.short: Education as investment and consumption, human capital, costs, benefits, demand, supply and financing.

sections.heading: Investment and consumption
sections.text: Education is both an investment and a consumption good. It is consumption when people value learning, school life or a qualification for its own sake and enjoy benefits now. It is investment when people give up time and money now to gain benefits later, such as higher earnings, better health or wider choices. The human capital idea treats knowledge and skills as a stock that raises a person’s productivity. Schooling, training and experience build that stock. Returns are later benefit flows.

sections.heading: Costs and benefits
sections.text: Private costs fall on the learner or family: fees, books, transport and forgone earnings. Private benefits include higher pay and better job prospects. Social costs are costs to society as a whole, including public spending on schools and the output lost while students study. Social benefits add spillovers, such as a healthier population and faster economic growth, to private benefits. Example: a one-year course costs 40,000 in fees, 10,000 in books and transport, and 30,000 in forgone earnings. Private cost = 40,000 + 10,000 + 30,000 = 80,000. If it raises earnings by 20,000 a year for five years, private benefit = 100,000, so the simple surplus is 20,000. This ignores discounting, risk and taxes.

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.text: Demand for education comes from households and employers. It rises with expected returns, school quality and family income, and falls with fees and distance. Supply depends on teachers, buildings, equipment and funding. In the short run, places are limited. Because education creates social benefits and poor families may not be able to borrow, markets alone may provide too little. Governments therefore regulate, fund or provide education.

sections.heading: Financing basics
sections.text: Education is financed from several sources: public taxes, fees, donations, loans and school income. Cost-sharing means government, families and students share the cost. Subsidies lower the price to users; grants and scholarships target support; loans spread payment over time; vouchers give families purchasing power. Each choice affects who attends, quality and fairness. Countries differ; check current national policy.

keyPoints: Education is both consumption, enjoyed now, and investment, costing now for later returns.
Human capital is the stock of skills and knowledge that raises productivity.
Private cost = fees + books and transport + forgone earnings; social cost adds public spending and lost output.
Private benefit = extra earnings and job prospects; social benefit adds spillovers such as health and growth.
Simple private surplus = private benefit − private cost, before discounting and risk.
Demand depends on expected returns, fees, income and quality; supply depends on teachers, facilities and funding; financing comes from taxes, fees, donations, loans and school income.

en.title: Educational Statistics and Data
en.short: Percentages, averages, ratios, enrolment indicators, data quality and reading tables and charts.

sections.heading: Describing numbers
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise data without generalising beyond them. A percentage compares a part with a whole: part ÷ whole × 100. If 45 of 180 pupils are girls, the share is 45 ÷ 180 × 100 = 25%. A ratio compares two quantities, written as a:b or as a quotient; it is not a percentage. If a school has 300 pupils and 15 teachers, the pupil-teacher ratio is 300:15, or 20:1.

An average represents a set. The mean adds all values and divides by their number. The median is the middle value when values are ordered. The mode is the most frequent value. The mean is pulled by extremes; the median is more resistant to outliers.

sections.heading: Enrolment indicators
sections.text:
Educational managers use enrolment indicators to compare access and staffing. The gross enrolment ratio (GER) is total enrolment at a level, whatever pupils’ ages, divided by the official school-age population, times 100. The net enrolment ratio (NER) counts only official-age pupils, divided by the same population, times 100. Official school ages differ by country, so check the current national source.

Worked example, invented: a district has 12,000 children of official primary school age. Primary enrolment is 9,600 pupils, of whom 7,200 are of official age. GER = 9,600 ÷ 12,000 × 100 = 80%. NER = 7,200 ÷ 12,000 × 100 = 60%. With 240 teachers, the pupil-teacher ratio is 9,600 ÷ 240 = 40 pupils per teacher.

sections.heading: Data quality and charts
sections.text: Good data are accurate, complete, timely and consistent. Accuracy means correct counts; completeness means no missing schools or pupils; timeliness means data are current enough for decisions; consistency means the same definitions are used across years and places. Record the source, date and definitions. A table should have a clear title, units and totals that add up. In a chart, read the axes, scale and labels before judging a trend. A truncated axis can exaggerate small changes. Missing data should be shown, not hidden.

keyPoints: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100.
Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; the median is the middle ordered value and the mode is the most frequent value.
Ratio compares two quantities and is not a percentage.
GER = total enrolment ÷ official school-age population × 100; NER = official-age enrolment ÷ official school-age population × 100.
Pupil-teacher ratio = pupils ÷ teachers.
Check data for accuracy, completeness, timeliness and consistency, and read chart axes and scales before drawing conclusions.

en.title: Educational Leadership Theories
en.short: Trait, behavioural, transformational, instructional, distributed and servant leadership in schools.

sections.heading: Leadership and management
sections.text: Leadership is the process of influencing people to set and achieve shared goals. Management is the process of planning, organising, coordinating and controlling resources so that work is done reliably. A school headteacher needs both: leadership to shape direction and commitment, management to keep timetables, budgets and records working. The two overlap, but a good manager is not automatically a good leader, and a visionary leader may manage poorly.

sections.heading: Trait and behavioural
sections.text: Trait theory asks whether leaders share personal qualities such as confidence, integrity or decisiveness. It explains some differences but underestimates context and training, and lists of traits vary. Behavioural theory studies what leaders do. It separates task behaviour, which structures work, from relationship behaviour, which supports people. In a school, task behaviour appears in clear lesson-observation schedules; relationship behaviour appears in listening to a teacher after a difficult class.

sections.heading: Transformational and instructional
sections.text: Transformational leadership raises expectations and builds commitment through an inspiring vision, individual support and intellectual stimulation. Instructional leadership focuses directly on teaching and learning: setting learning goals, coordinating the curriculum and observing teaching. A head who runs weekly coaching walks and also explains a shared vision is using both. Transformational theory can inspire change; instructional theory keeps attention on classroom learning.

sections.heading: Distributed and servant
sections.text: Distributed leadership treats leadership as shared across formal and informal roles, not held only by the head. Servant leadership puts followers first: the leader serves their growth and needs. Example: in a school facing weak mathematics results, a head may set the goal (transformational), lead lesson reviews (instructional), give department heads responsibility for planning (distributed), and ask what support teachers need (servant). Trait and behavioural ideas still help describe the people and actions involved.

keyPoints: Leadership influences direction and commitment; management coordinates resources and routines.
Trait theory looks for personal qualities, but context and training also matter.
Behavioural theory separates task-focused and relationship-focused actions.
Transformational leadership builds vision and commitment; instructional leadership focuses on teaching and learning.
Distributed leadership shares responsibility across roles; servant leadership puts followers’ needs first.
School leaders usually combine theories rather than rely on one.

en.title: School Administration and Management
en.short: How heads, committees and routines run the school day through decisions, delegation, meetings and time management.

sections.heading: The daily work
sections.text:
School administration is the day-to-day coordination of people, time and tasks so that lessons can proceed. Management is often used to mean the same work; writers differ on how the two terms differ. The head, called head teacher or principal depending on the country and school level, is accountable for this work, but duties vary by school type. Deputies, heads of department, class teachers and office staff carry out parts of it.

A school committee is a small group given a defined task, such as the timetable, co-curricular activities or staff welfare. Its terms of reference state whether it advises the head or decides. Committees widen consultation, but they need clear membership, a chair and a reporting line.

sections.heading: Decisions and delegation
sections.text:
Decision making means choosing between possible courses of action. A simple sequence is: clarify the issue, gather facts, consult those affected, decide, communicate the decision, then review it. Record who decided and why.

Delegation means entrusting a task and the authority to do it to another person. The head remains accountable. Match the task to the person’s skill, state the expected result, deadline and resources, and agree how progress will be checked. Delegation is not abdication: the head still supports and follows up.

sections.heading: Meetings and time
sections.text:
Meetings coordinate work. A useful meeting has a clear purpose, an agenda sent in advance, a chair who keeps to time, and minutes that list decisions and actions with owners and dates. Invite only people who need to be there. Start and end on time.

Time management means deciding what matters most and protecting time for it. Heads use the school timetable, a weekly calendar and short daily briefings to handle routine matters. They set aside uninterrupted time for classroom observation and planning, and deal with interruptions through agreed channels rather than constant open access.

sections.heading: Routines and learning
sections.text: Routines support teaching when predictable. In an invented case, Principal Adeyemi delegates a timetable review to her deputy. A short staff meeting agrees to publish changes weekly and brief teachers daily. Lessons start calmly because information arrives before teachers need it.

keyPoints: School administration coordinates daily people, time and tasks so teaching can proceed.
A school committee needs clear terms of reference, membership, a chair and a reporting line.
Decision making follows a cycle from clarifying the issue to reviewing the choice.
Delegation gives a task and authority but the head remains accountable.
Useful meetings have an agenda, minutes and actions with owners and dates.
Predictable routines protect teaching time and reduce disruption.

en.title: Human Resource Management in Education
en.short: Recruitment, selection, induction, appraisal, discipline, motivation and labour relations for school staff.

sections.heading: Staffing cycle
sections.text: Human resource management (HRM) is the planned management of people so that an education institution meets its goals. Recruitment attracts applicants; selection chooses among them using job descriptions, interviews, references and, where used, tests. Induction introduces a new staff member to the school’s routines, policies and colleagues. Deployment assigns staff to classes, subjects or duties according to qualifications and need. In a case, a district office advertises two science posts, shortlists five candidates, checks references, and inducts the two appointed teachers before term starts. Employment law, qualification rules and public-service procedures vary by country, so managers must follow the current national and local regulations.

sections.heading: Appraisal and development
sections.text: Appraisal is the regular review of a staff member’s work against agreed standards. It should use evidence such as lesson observation, records and results, and end with targets. Staff development means planned learning, including workshops, mentoring, further study and peer support. Appraisal and development link when a review identifies a training need. A fair system separates support from punishment and gives the person a chance to respond.

sections.heading: Discipline and motivation
sections.text: Discipline is the fair correction of conduct that breaks agreed rules, or performance that falls below agreed standards. It requires clear rules, notice of the allegation, a hearing, and a right of appeal; serious cases may follow national procedures. Motivation is what energises staff to work well. It can be extrinsic, such as pay and promotion, or intrinsic, such as recognition, autonomy and meaningful work. A head who thanks staff publicly and shares timetabling decisions fairly is using recognition and giving staff a say, not only money.

sections.heading: Labour relations
sections.text: Labour relations, also called industrial relations, is the management of the relationship between employers and staff or their unions. It covers consultation, collective bargaining (negotiation over pay and conditions), grievance handling and dispute resolution. Managers should keep records, meet representatives honestly and follow agreed procedures. Employment rules, union rights and dismissal procedures differ by country and sector; check the current labour law, education service rules and any collective agreement.

keyPoints: Recruitment attracts applicants; selection chooses the best fit against clear criteria.
Induction and deployment help new and existing staff work effectively.
Appraisal reviews performance against standards and should link to staff development.
Discipline needs clear rules, a fair hearing and a right of appeal.
Motivation includes extrinsic rewards such as pay and intrinsic factors such as recognition and autonomy.
Labour relations cover consultation, collective bargaining, grievances and disputes, and employment rules vary by country.

en.title: Educational Finance and Budgeting
en.short: Sources of education funds, the budget cycle, cost control, financial records, audit and accountability.

sections.heading: Sources of funds
sections.text: Educational finance is the management of money for schools and colleges. Funds come from public sources, such as government grants and tax-funded budgets; from private sources, such as fees, donations and endowments, which are invested gifts; and from internal income, such as rentals or a school farm. Loans and partnerships also exist. Recurrent funds pay day-to-day costs; capital funds pay for buildings and equipment. The mix varies by country and institution, so check the current official rules.

sections.heading: Budgeting process
sections.text: A budget is a plan in money for a set period. The cycle is: estimate income, estimate expenditure, consult staff, draft, get approval, implement, monitor and review. Line-item budgets list each expense; programme budgets group spending by activity; zero-based budgets start from zero each year. In an invented example, a school plans income of 500,000 currency units and spending of 480,000, a surplus of 20,000. Actual income is 450,000 and spending 470,000, a deficit of 20,000. Spending is 10,000 under budget (470,000 − 480,000 = −10,000).

sections.heading: Cost control and records
sections.text: Cost control compares actual results with the budget, explains variances and acts. A variance is the difference between planned and actual figures. Financial records include the cash book, ledger (the main accounts book), receipts, payment vouchers, payroll and asset register. Good internal control separates duties, requires authorisation, checks bank statements against the cash book and keeps records safe. These controls reduce the risk of loss and make the audit trail clear. An audit trail lets each transaction be traced from source to report.

sections.heading: Audit and accountability
sections.text: An audit is an independent check of financial records and controls. Internal auditors work within the organisation; external auditors report to governing bodies or owners. Accountability means explaining how funds were used and accepting responsibility. Managers should report regularly, answer questions and correct weaknesses. Audited accounts and clear records build trust with funders, parents and regulators.

keyPoints: Educational funds are recurrent or capital, and may come from public, private and internal sources.
The budget cycle runs from estimating income and expenditure through approval and implementation to monitoring and review.
Surplus or deficit = income − expenditure; in the example, 450,000 − 470,000 = −20,000, a deficit.
Variance = actual − budget; a negative spending variance means underspending, a positive one means overspending.
Financial records and internal controls create an audit trail and reduce the risk of loss.
Audit is an independent check, while accountability means explaining and answering for the use of funds.

en.title: School Plant and Facilities Management
en.short: Site choice, buildings, classrooms, furniture, maintenance, safety and space use in schools.

sections.heading: Site and buildings
sections.text:
School plant means the land, buildings, furniture, equipment and services a school uses. Site selection is the choice of land. A good site is large enough for enrolment and expansion, well drained, free from flooding, noise, pollution and traffic danger, and has safe access, water and power. Local planning and building rules vary by country, so managers check current official requirements.

Buildings should be durable, well ventilated, lit, accessible and flexible. They must meet fire and structural safety codes. A cheap but poorly ventilated building raises illness and fatigue and weakens teaching.

sections.heading: Classrooms and furniture
sections.text: Classrooms need enough space per learner, clear sightlines, good acoustics, natural light and cross-ventilation. Layout should allow whole-class teaching, group work and movement. Furniture means desks, chairs, tables and storage. It should suit learners’ age and size, be sturdy and safe, and be adjustable where possible. Poor furniture causes discomfort and poor posture. Enough furniture for the enrolment prevents crowding and lost teaching time.

sections.heading: Maintenance and safety
sections.text: Maintenance keeps facilities usable. Preventive maintenance is planned work such as painting, servicing and roof checks. Corrective maintenance repairs faults after they appear. Keep an inspection schedule, a fault log and a budget. Safety covers fire exits, extinguishers, first aid, clean water, toilets, electrical checks, security and emergency drills. Managers should close or repair unsafe areas at once. Facilities management therefore protects health and safety and supports effective teaching.

sections.heading: Space utilisation
sections.text: Space utilisation means how fully rooms and seats are used. Room use rate is periods used divided by periods available. Seat occupancy is learners present divided by designed capacity. Example: a school has 20 classrooms, each available for 30 periods a week; 24 periods are used, so room use is 24 ÷ 30 = 80%. A room designed for 40 holds 36 learners, so seat occupancy is 36 ÷ 40 = 90%. Combined use is 0.80 × 0.90 = 72%. Timetabling and class-size planning raise use without overcrowding.

keyPoints: School plant covers land, buildings, furniture, equipment and services.
Site selection weighs size, drainage, hazards, access, utilities, expansion and local rules.
Classrooms need space, light, ventilation, acoustics and flexible layouts.
Furniture should be safe, durable, age-appropriate and sufficient for enrolment.
Preventive maintenance is planned; corrective maintenance repairs faults after they appear.
Space utilisation equals room use rate × seat occupancy, as in 80% × 90% = 72%.

en.title: Curriculum and Instructional Management
en.short: Implementing curriculum, schemes of work, timetables, materials and supportive lesson oversight.

sections.heading: Curriculum implementation
sections.text: Curriculum implementation is the process of turning an approved curriculum into classroom learning. It includes interpreting aims and content, preparing teachers, providing resources, and checking that learners meet the intended outcomes. Managers coordinate this work, but teachers adapt examples, pace and methods to their classes. Local rules on curriculum approval differ by country, so check the current official syllabus.

sections.heading: Schemes and timetables
sections.text: A scheme of work breaks the syllabus into units across a term or year. It usually states objectives, content, activities, resources and assessment for each week or unit. A timetable allocates time, rooms and teachers. It should protect curriculum time, avoid clashes, and allow double periods for practical work where needed. Both are planning tools, not fixed scripts; review them when learners need more time.

sections.heading: Materials and lesson plans
sections.text: Instructional materials are resources that support learning, such as textbooks, charts, laboratory equipment, local objects and digital content. Choose them for alignment with objectives, accuracy, accessibility and cost. A lesson plan sets out intended learning, prior knowledge, activities, materials and assessment for one lesson. Managers review plans for coherence and coverage, then discuss improvements with the teacher.

sections.heading: Monitoring and support
sections.text: Monitoring instruction means gathering evidence about teaching and learning through brief classroom visits, samples of learners’ work, record checks and meetings. The purpose is support, not control. In an invented case, Mrs Adeyemi, a head of department in Ibadan, notices a teacher’s scheme is behind. She asks what support is needed, arranges a shared resource, and agrees a revised pace. She does not rewrite the lesson plan. Professional judgement stays with the teacher; managers ensure clear alignment, resources and fair accountability.

keyPoints: Curriculum implementation turns an approved curriculum into classroom learning through interpretation, resources and checks on outcomes.
A scheme of work sequences syllabus content over a term or year; a timetable allocates time, rooms and teachers.
Instructional materials should match objectives and be accurate, accessible and affordable.
A lesson plan sets out intended learning, activities, materials and assessment for one lesson.
Managers monitor through visits, work samples and records, and use findings to support teachers.
Oversight should protect curriculum coverage and fairness without replacing teachers’ professional judgement.

en.title: Educational Supervision and Inspection
en.short: Supervision and inspection compared, clinical supervision, feedback, teacher support and school improvement.

sections.heading: Two different purposes
sections.text:
Supervision is the internal, continuous process of guiding teachers to improve teaching and learning. It is usually formative: its purpose is support and development, not judgement. Inspection is external and periodic. An inspectorate checks whether a school meets stated standards and reports judgements for accountability. Inspection is therefore summative and compliance-focused.

The two overlap. A supervisor may be a head of department or senior teacher; an inspector comes from outside. Supervision builds trust and daily improvement; inspection protects public standards. Systems differ by country, so check local guidance.

sections.heading: Clinical supervision cycle
sections.text:
Clinical supervision is a structured, collaborative cycle. It has three main stages: a pre-observation conference where teacher and supervisor agree the lesson focus; classroom observation with a written record; and a post-observation conference where they analyse evidence and plan action. The teacher sets goals, so the process is teacher-centred.

Case: In Ibadan, Nigeria, Mrs Adeyemi asks her head of department to observe a chemistry lesson on mole calculations. They focus on checking every student’s work. The supervisor notes six students finished early and waited. They plan a short extension task, and a follow-up visit checks it.

sections.heading: Feedback and support
sections.text:
Effective feedback is specific, timely and based on evidence, not personality. It describes what happened, explains its effect on learning, and suggests one or two next steps. “You gave three examples” is stronger than “good lesson”. Feedback should be a dialogue: the teacher explains decisions and agrees the action.

Support follows through coaching, mentoring, resources, training and protected time. Without follow-up, supervision becomes a ritual.

sections.heading: Quality control and improvement
sections.text:
Quality control asks whether minimum standards are met: safety, records, curriculum coverage, teacher qualifications and learning outcomes. Inspection supplies an external check and can trigger intervention. Supervision supplies the everyday evidence and support that make improvement possible.

School improvement links both to a plan: analyse evidence, choose priorities, act, then review. Neither inspection nor supervision improves a school by itself; improvement depends on what staff do with the findings.

keyPoints: Supervision is internal, continuous and formative; inspection is external, periodic and summative.
Inspection checks compliance with standards, while supervision supports daily teaching and learning.
Clinical supervision follows pre-observation, observation and post-observation stages, with agreed goals.
Effective feedback is specific, evidence-based, timely and followed by support such as coaching.
Quality control uses inspection evidence to check minimum standards and trigger action.
School improvement depends on how staff act on supervision and inspection findings.

en.title: Quality Assurance in Education
en.short: Standards, internal and external quality assurance, accreditation, indicators and school improvement.

sections.heading: Standards and quality
sections.text: Quality assurance is the planned process of checking and improving whether education meets agreed standards. A standard is a written statement of the level expected, for example what a graduate should know or how a school should be run. Quality control checks outputs after the event; quality assurance builds checks into everyday work. A quality culture means staff and students share responsibility for improvement, not only compliance with rules.

sections.heading: Internal and external QA
sections.text: Internal quality assurance is what a school or college does itself: self-evaluation, lesson observation, moderation of assessment, student feedback and review of records. External quality assurance is done by an outside body: inspection, programme review, audit or accreditation. External review can validate internal claims and compare institutions, but it should support improvement, not only judge. Both need evidence, clear criteria and honest reporting.

sections.heading: Accreditation and indicators
sections.text: Accreditation is formal recognition that an institution or programme meets stated standards, usually for a fixed period and subject to renewal. It may be institutional or programme-based. Performance indicators are measures used to judge quality, such as pass rates, attendance, teacher qualifications, completion and progression. They are useful but incomplete: a high pass rate may reflect easy marking or selective admission. Use several indicators and compare like with like.

sections.heading: School improvement
sections.text: School improvement is a cycle: gather evidence, identify priorities, plan action, implement it, then review the effect. An invented case: at a fictional secondary school, low attendance and weak mathematics results lead the head to set two targets, monitor them termly, and report to the board. Quality assurance bodies and requirements vary by country and sector. Check the current official agency and rules for your own country.

keyPoints: Quality assurance checks and improves whether education meets agreed standards.
A standard states the expected level of knowledge, practice or provision.
Internal quality assurance is school-based; external quality assurance is done by an outside body.
Accreditation is formal recognition that an institution or programme meets stated standards.
Performance indicators are useful but must be read together and in context.
School improvement follows a cycle of evidence, priorities, action and review, and quality assurance requirements vary by country.

en.title: Educational Policy and Reform
en.short: The policy cycle, stakeholder roles, and why education reforms succeed or fail.

sections.heading: The policy cycle
sections.text: A policy is a decision or set of decisions that guides action and allocates resources. The policy cycle is a model, not a fixed sequence. Formulation defines the problem, sets goals, compares options, consults, and decides. Implementation turns the decision into plans, budgets, staffing, rules and school practice. Analysis is the systematic appraisal of options and effects; it can happen before a decision, as ex ante analysis, or after, as evaluation. Evaluation compares outputs and outcomes with goals and feeds lessons into the next cycle.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and analysis
sections.text: Stakeholders are the people and groups affected by a policy or able to affect it. In education they include teachers and their unions, school leaders, parents, students, employers, civil society, and officials. Involvement improves information and ownership, but it can slow decisions and favour loud groups. Good analysis asks who gains, who loses, what it costs, and whether schools have the capacity to deliver. It uses data, but data are often incomplete, so judgement is needed.

sections.heading: Why reforms fail
sections.text: Reforms succeed when goals are clear, resources match tasks, roles are defined, school leaders have capacity, and monitoring allows correction. They fail when they are top-down, underfunded, rushed, poorly communicated, or captured by political turnover. The implementation gap is the distance between an adopted policy and classroom practice. It grows when teachers receive no training, when budgets arrive late, or when no one checks results. Success is rarely automatic; it depends on ownership and steady support.

sections.heading: Country variation
sections.text: Legal frameworks vary by country. Who controls curriculum, teacher employment and funding differs, and federal states may share education between national and state bodies. Policy examples also vary by year, so check current official sources. In an invented case, a state ministry led by Amina announces free primary education without funding textbooks. Enrolment rises, but teachers lack materials and classes grow. After evaluation, the ministry phases textbook grants and consults head teachers before the next step.

keyPoints: The policy cycle links formulation, implementation, analysis and evaluation, and it is a model rather than a fixed sequence.
Stakeholders include teachers, unions, parents, students, employers and officials; their involvement improves ownership but can slow decisions.
Policy analysis asks who gains, who loses, what it costs and whether schools can deliver.
Reforms succeed with clear goals, resources, capacity, defined roles and monitoring; they fail when top-down, underfunded or poorly communicated.
The implementation gap is the distance between adopted policy and classroom practice.
Legal frameworks and policy examples vary by country and year, so check current official sources.

en.title: Educational Law and School Governance
en.short: School legal frameworks, rights, discipline, liability and board governance roles.

sections.heading: Legal framework
sections.text: Education law is the body of constitutional provisions, statutes, regulations, case law and school policies that govern schools. It covers who may establish a school, what must be taught, admission, records, health and safety, and reporting. A right to education may be constitutional or statutory, but its scope and remedies differ by country. Duties fall on the state, owners, boards, head teachers, teachers and parents. Check the current national education act, state or provincial rules and local policy, because law and regulation are country-specific.

sections.heading: Discipline and liability
sections.text: Discipline must be lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair. Procedural fairness means telling the student the allegation, giving a chance to respond, using an impartial decision maker and allowing review. Corporal punishment is banned in many countries but not all; check the law. Liability is legal responsibility for harm. Schools owe a duty of care. Negligence usually needs a duty, a breach, damage and a close causal link. Vicarious liability can make an employer responsible for staff acts in the course of employment. Insurance and reporting duties vary.

sections.heading: Boards and governance
sections.text: Governance is direction, oversight and accountability. Management is day-to-day running. A school board, board of governors or management committee sets strategy, approves budgets, appoints and appraises the head, monitors results and ensures compliance. It should not run daily teaching. Members need clear terms of reference, conflict-of-interest rules and minutes. Boards may be elected or appointed, and their powers differ by country.

sections.heading: Case and compliance
sections.text: Suppose a student at a secondary school in Lagos is suspended after a fight. The head should follow the school’s written procedure and any state or national rules: record the allegation, hear the student and parents, consider evidence, impose a proportionate sanction and allow appeal. Skipping the hearing can make an otherwise justified suspension unfair. Statutory requirements such as registration, safety, attendance records and safeguarding must be checked against current official sources.

keyPoints: Education law is country-specific; check national acts, regulations and school policy.
Schools owe a duty of care, and negligence usually needs duty, breach, damage and causation.
Discipline must be lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair.
Vicarious liability can make an employer responsible for staff acts in employment.
Governance sets direction and oversight, while management runs daily operations.
School boards approve budgets, appoint heads, monitor results and ensure compliance.

en.title: School Records and Information Management
en.short: Types of school records, storage, confidentiality, data protection and education management information systems.

sections.heading: Types of records
sections.text: A school record is information kept about the school, its staff or its students for later use. Admission records include application forms, the admission register and evidence of age or prior schooling. Attendance records include the daily register, absence notes and attendance summaries. Personnel records include staff files, contracts, qualifications and appraisal reports. Financial records include budgets, ledgers, receipts, invoices, payroll and bank statements. Each type supports a different decision: who is enrolled, who is present, how staff are managed and how money is received and spent.

sections.heading: Storage and protection
sections.text: Storage must protect records from loss, damage and unauthorised access. Paper records need locked cabinets and a dry room. Electronic records need passwords, access levels, backups and protection from malware. A retention schedule states how long each record is kept and how it is destroyed. Confidentiality means sharing personal information only with people who need it for their work. Data protection is the legal and ethical duty to collect personal data for a lawful purpose, keep it accurate and secure, retain it no longer than necessary, and respect people’s rights. Laws differ by country; in Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 applies. Check the current official source.

sections.heading: EMIS in practice
sections.text: An education management information system (EMIS) is a computer-based system for collecting, storing, analysing and reporting education data. A school may use EMIS for enrolment, attendance, staffing, finance and results. Good data help managers plan classrooms, teachers and budgets, and help authorities compare schools. The system is only as good as its data: staff must enter records promptly and check them. Example: at a secondary school in Kano, the clerk records attendance daily. In a month with 20 school days and 500 students, possible attendances are 500 × 20 = 10,000. If 9,200 attendances are recorded, the rate is 9,200 ÷ 10,000 = 0.92, or 92%. The school can investigate absence and plan support.

keyPoints: School records include admission, attendance, personnel and financial records.
Store records securely in locked cabinets or password-protected systems, with backups and a retention schedule.
Confidentiality limits personal information to people who need it for their work.
Data protection requires lawful purpose, accuracy, security, limited retention and respect for rights; laws differ by country.
An EMIS collects, stores, analyses and reports education data for planning and management.
Attendance rate = recorded attendances ÷ possible attendances × 100, where possible attendances = students × school days.

en.title: Educational Change and Innovation
en.short: How schools plan change, handle resistance, adopt innovations and integrate technology.

sections.heading: The change process
sections.text: Educational change is a planned shift in structures, practices or beliefs. Innovation is an idea, method or tool that is new to the school, even if used elsewhere. A common model is Lewin’s three stages: unfreeze, change and refreeze. Unfreezing creates readiness by showing a problem and a vision. The change stage trials new practice with support. Refreezing embeds it in routines, budgets and training. Kotter’s eight steps stress urgency, a guiding team, short-term wins and communication, while Rogers’ diffusion of innovations explains how new ideas spread through a community over time. Treat models as guides, not rigid recipes.

sections.heading: Resistance and adoption
sections.text: Resistance is not stubbornness. It can come from fear of loss, extra workload, weak communication, past failed reforms or lack of resources. Adoption also varies: Rogers describes innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards. Leaders should listen, explain the reason, involve teachers in design, offer training and remove practical barriers. For example, in an invented case, Mrs Adeyemi, principal of a Nigerian secondary school, wants continuous assessment records online. She starts with two volunteer teachers, shares a simple template, and gives time. Early wins build trust before whole-school rollout.

sections.heading: Leading change
sections.text: Managing change means planning, coordinating and sustaining it. Leaders set a clear aim, assign responsibilities, provide resources and monitor effects. They should protect time for professional development and allow feedback. Sustainable improvement lasts after the leader leaves, so it must sit in school routines, job descriptions and budgets, not depend on one person. Evaluate with evidence, such as attendance, teacher use or learner work, and adjust.

sections.heading: Technology and sustainability
sections.text: Technology integration is change, not purchase. A device or platform helps only when it fits the curriculum, the timetable and teachers’ skills. Leaders should check infrastructure, data protection and total cost, including maintenance and connectivity. Start small, train teachers, offer technical support and review. In the case, Mrs Adeyemi could pilot the records system for one term, compare accuracy and time saved, then decide. This is evidence-based, sustainable change.

keyPoints: Change is a planned shift in structures, practices or beliefs; innovation is something new to the school.
Lewin’s unfreeze, change and refreeze model, Kotter’s steps and Rogers’ diffusion model are guides, not rigid recipes.
Resistance often reflects fear, workload, poor communication or past failures, so leaders should listen and involve staff.
Adoption spreads from innovators and early adopters to the majority, so piloting with volunteers can build trust.
Sustainable improvement is embedded in routines, budgets and job descriptions and is evaluated with evidence.
Technology integration needs curriculum fit, training, infrastructure, data protection and total cost, not just devices.

en.title: School and Community Relations
en.short: Parents, PTAs, community partners, communication, conflict handling and social responsibility.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and parents
sections.text: School and community relations are the planned links between a school and outside people and groups. Parents are the first stakeholders, meaning people with an interest in the school. Parental involvement includes helping at home, attending meetings and joining activities. A parent-teacher association (PTA) is a formal body of parents and teachers. Its powers vary by country and school, so check local policy. Community groups include alumni, employers, clinics, religious and traditional bodies, and non-governmental organisations. Partners bring resources, skills or placements. Partnership means shared goals and clear roles, not a one-way donation.

sections.heading: Communication and partnership
sections.text: Communication should be two-way, regular and accessible. Schools use notices, meetings, phone calls, text messages and local languages. Share good news and problems early. Partnership needs a clear understanding of aims, roles, resources, safeguarding (protecting learners from harm) and reporting. For example, in a fictional town, a school and a local clinic agree to run health talks. A teacher coordinates dates, the clinic sends a nurse, and both review attendance. This is partnership because each side contributes and learns.

sections.heading: Handling conflict
sections.text: Conflict is normal. Handle it early, privately and fairly. Listen to each side, separate facts from feelings, record what was said, and agree next steps. A neutral person, such as a PTA officer or local education officer, may mediate. In a fictional case, a parent, Mrs Okafor, complains that a school levy was not explained. The head teacher meets her, shows the budget records, explains each item, and the PTA forms a committee to check future spending. Trust improves because the process is open.

sections.heading: Social responsibility
sections.text: A school has a social responsibility to the community: a safe environment, fair access, honest reporting and respect for local values. It should care for the environment and, where policy allows, share facilities. The community should support the school with respect and constructive feedback. Social responsibility is not public relations only; it is daily conduct that earns trust.

keyPoints: School and community relations are planned, two-way links with parents, groups and partners.
Parents are the first stakeholders, and a PTA is a formal parent-teacher body whose rules vary by country and school.
Good communication is regular, accessible and two-way, and shares problems early.
Partnership requires shared goals, clear roles, resources, safeguarding and reporting.
Handle conflict early, privately and fairly, using records and a neutral mediator if needed.
Social responsibility means safe, fair, honest conduct and respect for local values, not just publicity.

en.title: Comparative and International Education Management
en.short: How to compare education systems, governance, accountability, access and quality across countries.

sections.heading: Comparing systems
sections.text:
Comparative education is the systematic study of similarities and differences between education systems. International education looks across borders, including aid, exchange and policy borrowing.

To compare management, ask four questions: who owns and funds schools, who employs teachers, who sets the curriculum, and who assesses learning. A central ministry may control all four, or authority may be split between national, state, district and school bodies. These arrangements vary by country and history, so no single model is universal.

sections.heading: Decentralisation and accountability
sections.text:
Decentralisation means moving authority from a central ministry to districts, schools or communities. Devolution transfers legal power to local bodies; deconcentration moves tasks to local offices that remain under the ministry. School-based management gives schools control over budgets or staffing.

Accountability means being answerable for results. It can run through inspection, public exams, audits, parent boards or performance reports. Decentralisation may improve local fit but can widen inequality where local capacity or funding is weak. In an invented case, Amina’s district in northern Nigeria sets school budgets while a national board pays teachers; Kwame’s school board in Ghana hires staff. A manager comparing them must check legal authority, money flow and who answers to whom.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and quality
sections.text:
International benchmarks are common measures used to compare systems. The OECD’s PISA tests 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics and science; it does not cover every country. The UN’s Sustainable Development Goal 4 sets global education aims. Regional assessments include SACMEQ in southern and eastern Africa and PASEC in francophone Africa.

Benchmarks are useful but limited: sampling, language, curriculum and culture affect results, and league tables can mislead. Access means who gets into education and stays; quality concerns inputs, teaching and learning outcomes. Compare both, and adapt borrowed policies to local law, money and capacity rather than copying one country’s practice.

keyPoints: Comparative education studies similarities and differences between systems; international education looks across borders.
Compare management by asking who owns, funds, employs, sets curriculum and assesses learning.
Decentralisation transfers authority; devolution is legal transfer, while deconcentration is administrative.
Accountability can use inspection, exams, audits and parent boards, but local control may widen inequality.
PISA, SDG 4, SACMEQ and PASEC are benchmarks, not universal standards.
Access and quality must be compared together, and borrowed policies adapted to local context.

en.title: Educational Ethics and Professionalism
en.short: Ethical principles, conflicts of interest and professional codes in educational management.

sections.heading: Ethics in management
sections.text: Ethics means standards of right conduct. In educational management, decisions affect learners, staff, families and public funds, so managers need more than efficiency. Fairness means treating like cases alike, using published criteria and giving reasons for decisions. Integrity means honesty, keeping promises and keeping records accurate. Accountability means being answerable for choices: recording the reasons, explaining them and accepting review. These principles guide judgement, but they do not replace the law, regulations or employer policy.

sections.heading: Conflicts of interest
sections.text:
A conflict of interest exists when a private interest or relationship could improperly influence an official decision. It may be actual, potential or perceived. The usual response is to declare it early and in writing, then step away from the decision. Recusal means withdrawing from the decision and its discussion. Keep a record of the declaration and who decided instead.

Case: Principal Amina, in Kano, Nigeria, chairs a committee choosing a textbook supplier. Her brother owns one bidder. She declares the relationship, leaves the meeting and lets the deputy chair the committee, which applies the published criteria. The outcome may be the same, but the process is now defensible and fair.

sections.heading: Professional codes
sections.text: A professional code is a written statement of the conduct expected of members. Codes commonly require duty of care, respect, confidentiality, honesty and the reporting of misconduct. They vary by country and by body. Some countries have a teaching council; others regulate teachers through a ministry or agency. In Nigeria, the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) is the teacher regulatory body, and its current code should be checked. A code supports professionalism, which means competent and ethical practice, but it is not a substitute for law or employer policy.

keyPoints: Ethics in educational management concerns fairness, integrity and accountability, not only efficiency.
Fairness uses consistent, published criteria and gives reasons for decisions.
Integrity requires honest records and kept promises.
Accountability means explaining decisions and accepting review.
A conflict of interest should be declared early, recorded, and the person should recuse.
Professional codes vary by country; check the current code of your regulator and employer policy.

en.title: Research Methods in Educational Management
en.short: Basic research designs, sampling, instruments, validity, reliability, ethics, simple analysis and report writing.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text:
Research design is the plan for answering a question. Common small-study designs in education are surveys, which describe opinions or conditions; case studies, which examine one school or office in depth; and quasi-experiments, which compare groups without random assignment. Choose the design that fits the question, not the easiest one.

Sampling means selecting part of a population, the whole group you want to describe. A sample is the selected part. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection and supports generalisation. Purposive sampling selects people for a reason, such as heads with budget experience, and does not support statistical generalisation.

sections.heading: Instruments and quality
sections.text:
An instrument is the tool for collecting data, such as a questionnaire, interview guide or observation checklist. Keep questions short, neutral and unambiguous. Pilot the instrument on a few people and revise it.

Validity means the instrument measures what it claims to measure. Reliability means it gives consistent results on repeated use or across items. A scale can be reliable but invalid if it measures the wrong thing. Use clear definitions, expert review and piloting to improve both.

sections.heading: Ethics and analysis
sections.text:
Ethics protect participants and the school. Obtain permission from the education authority and school head. Seek informed consent, explain purpose and use, allow withdrawal, and get parent or guardian consent for children. Keep identities confidential, or collect no names at all so data are anonymous. Avoid harm and do not fabricate or falsify data.

For simple analysis, use counts, percentages and means. If 24 of 40 teachers agree, the percentage is 24 ÷ 40 × 100 = 60%. The mean is the sum divided by the number of values. Qualitative data can be grouped into themes with short quotations.

sections.heading: Writing the report
