sections.text: Report writing follows a clear order: title, problem, aims, methods, findings, discussion, recommendations and references. State the sample size and limitations. Separate evidence from opinion. For a school study, give practical recommendations that follow from the findings. Check arithmetic and keep raw data for verification.

keyPoints: Research design is the plan for answering the question; surveys describe, case studies examine depth, and quasi-experiments compare groups without random assignment.
Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection; purposive sampling selects for a reason and does not support statistical generalisation.
Validity means measuring what is claimed; reliability means consistent results, and piloting improves both.
Ethics require permission, informed consent, parent or guardian consent for children, confidentiality or anonymity, and no harm.
Percentage = part ÷ total × 100; mean = sum ÷ number of values.
Reports state methods, findings, limitations and recommendations, and raw data should be kept for checking.

en.title: Advanced Theories of Educational Management
en.short: Critical, postmodern, feminist, complexity and institutional views of educational management.

sections.heading: Five perspectives
sections.text: Critical theory asks who benefits from a practice and whose interests it hides, tracing power to class, capital and ideology. Postmodernism, associated with Foucault and Lyotard, treats knowledge and order as produced by discourse, meaning language and accepted ways of speaking, so the school has no single truth. Feminist theory examines the gendered division of labour, care work and authority. Complexity theory sees schools as non-linear systems of interacting agents, where small changes can produce large effects. Institutional theory, associated with Meyer and Rowan, argues that organisations adopt formal structures to win legitimacy, not only efficiency, so policy and practice become loosely coupled, meaning stated rules and daily work drift apart.

sections.heading: Power and culture
sections.text: Each view defines power differently: as domination (critical), as dispersed and productive (postmodern), as gendered (feminist), as emergent (complexity), as legitimacy-seeking (institutional). Culture is therefore a site of struggle, not a shared banner. The practical question for a manager is whose voice is missing from the staff meeting, and what the timetable actually rewards.

sections.heading: Governance and change
sections.text: Critical and feminist views favour participation, voice and redress of inequality. Postmodern views distrust grand reform plans and prefer small, local, reversible moves. Complexity views favour experimenting, sensing and adjusting rather than rolling out one blueprint. Institutional views warn that a new policy may become a ceremonial document while classrooms stay unchanged.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: An invented case: a ministry requires every secondary school to submit a weekly lesson-completion report. A complexity reading expects teachers to adapt the form to their own routines. An institutional reading expects it to be completed for legitimacy while teaching continues much as before. A critical reading asks who is audited and who is not. The manager uses all three to predict what will actually happen.

keyPoints: Critical theory asks whose interests a management practice serves.
Postmodernism treats organisational truth as produced by discourse.
Feminist theory examines gendered power and care work in schools.
Complexity theory sees schools as non-linear systems where small changes can have large effects.
Institutional theory explains loose coupling between policy and classroom practice.
Each perspective implies a different approach to participation, governance and change.

en.title: Strategic Management in Education
en.short: Strategic analysis, vision, environmental scanning, strategy formulation and implementation in schools.

sections.heading: Strategy in schools
sections.text: Strategic management is the disciplined process of setting long-term direction for a school or system, choosing how to reach it, and reviewing progress. It differs from routine administration, which keeps current work running. Strategic analysis examines the organisation’s purpose, its external environment and its internal capacity. A vision states the desired future; a mission states the organisation’s present purpose and whom it serves. Both should be short enough to guide decisions, not slogans on a wall.

sections.heading: Scanning and analysis
sections.text: Environmental scanning collects information about trends outside the school: policy changes, population shifts, employer needs, technology and competition from other providers. Internal analysis reviews staff skills, finances, facilities and student outcomes. SWOT analysis is a simple tool that lists strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. It is a starting point, not a decision. In a case, Amina, principal of a college in Kano, Nigeria, finds employers asking for digital skills. Her scan shows strong teachers but few computers. That evidence shapes her strategy.

sections.heading: Formulation and choice
sections.text: Strategy formulation turns analysis into a few clear goals, priorities and actions. Leaders compare options against the vision, expected learning benefit, cost and feasibility. Resources are always limited, so a strategy must state what the school will stop or delay as well as what it will start. Accountability means being answerable for results to students, parents, funders and public authorities. Good strategies set measurable targets and assign responsibility without ignoring educational aims such as equity and breadth of learning.

sections.heading: Implementation and balance
sections.text: Implementation converts plans into budgets, staffing, timetables, training and monitoring. It needs clear owners, milestones and data. Review and adjust. The hard balance is between educational aims and resources. A school may want smaller classes, but the budget may not allow them. It can protect the aim through targeted tutoring or better use of time. Accountability should judge learning and equity, not only test scores or spending. In Kano, Amina phases in a computer laboratory, trains teachers and reports progress to the board.

keyPoints: Strategic management sets long-term direction and reviews progress, unlike routine administration.
A vision describes the desired future; a mission describes present purpose and whom the school serves.
Environmental scanning and SWOT analysis gather evidence but do not decide strategy.
Strategy formulation chooses priorities and states what will stop or delay when resources are limited.
Implementation needs budgets, owners, milestones, training and monitoring.
Accountability should judge learning and equity, not only test scores or spending.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Dissertation
en.short: Advanced designs, proposal writing, sampling, analysis, ethics and dissertation management.

sections.heading: Advanced designs
sections.text:
Master’s research goes beyond describing a problem. Quantitative designs test relationships with numbers, using surveys, experiments or existing datasets. Advanced analysis includes multiple regression, which estimates several predictors’ effects at once, and factor analysis, which groups related items. Qualitative designs explore meaning in context; common types are case study, phenomenology and grounded theory.

Mixed methods combine both. In a convergent design, quantitative and qualitative data are collected in parallel and merged; in an explanatory sequential design, qualitative work explains quantitative results. Integration links findings, not two separate studies.

sections.heading: Proposal and review
sections.text:
A proposal states the problem, research questions, design, sample, analysis plan, ethics and timeline. It must show a gap. A literature review synthesises relevant studies and explains how they lead to your question. A systematic review uses a fixed search protocol; a narrative review is selective.

Sampling must match the design. Probability sampling supports statistical generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or snowball, is common in qualitative work. Power analysis estimates the quantitative sample needed to detect an effect; saturation is the point when qualitative data add no new themes.

sections.heading: Analysis and example
sections.text:
Quantitative analysis uses descriptive and inferential statistics, such as regression, to estimate relationships and uncertainty. Qualitative analysis involves coding, which labels text segments, then thematic analysis, which groups codes into patterns. Software helps but does not replace judgement.

For example, imagine Ada, a master’s student in Oyo State, Nigeria, studying teacher supervision. She distributes 240 questionnaires and receives 180 back: 180 ÷ 240 = 0.75, a 75% response rate. She interviews 15 teachers purposively and stops when no new themes appear.

sections.heading: Ethics and management
sections.text:
Ethics approval is required before data collection. Informed consent means participants understand the purpose, risks, benefits and their right to withdraw. Protect confidentiality, store data securely and follow data protection rules.

A dissertation needs a realistic plan: supervisor meetings, Gantt chart of milestones, data management plan and backups. Word limits, deadlines and ethics forms vary by institution, so check your handbook.

keyPoints: Advanced quantitative analysis includes multiple regression and factor analysis; qualitative analysis uses coding and thematic analysis.
Mixed methods must integrate findings, not just collect two datasets.
A proposal states the problem, questions, design, sample, analysis plan, ethics and timeline.
Use power analysis for quantitative sample size and saturation for qualitative sampling.
Response rate = returned questionnaires ÷ distributed questionnaires × 100%.
Obtain ethics approval and informed consent before data collection, and check your institution’s handbook for deadlines and word limits.

en.title: Digital Transformation and Data-Driven Management
en.short: Digital tools, EMIS, learning analytics, data-informed decisions, benefits, risks, equity, privacy and change.

sections.heading: Digital tools and EMIS
sections.text: Digital transformation means using digital technology to change how work is done, not only buying devices. In education it includes school management software, online learning platforms, mobile data collection and education management information systems (EMIS). An EMIS is a system that collects, stores and reports data such as enrolment, attendance, staffing and results for planning and management. Data quality matters: incomplete or late returns mislead decisions. For example, if 8 of 10 schools send in their attendance returns, completeness is 8 ÷ 10 = 80%. A district can then target follow-up at the two missing schools.

sections.heading: Learning analytics
sections.text: Learning analytics is the measurement and analysis of learner data to understand and improve learning. It can flag students who miss classes or assignments, and it can show which topics need reteaching. A signal is not a diagnosis. If 40 of 200 students miss two assignments, that is 40 ÷ 200 = 20%, a group worth supporting. Teachers should ask why before acting, because absence may reflect transport, work or health, not low effort.

sections.heading: Benefits and risks
sections.text: Benefits include faster reporting, better planning, early support and less paperwork. Risks include poor data, cost, vendor lock-in, surveillance and bias. A dashboard can look objective while hiding missing groups. Digital tools can widen inequity when students lack electricity, connectivity, devices, disability access or local-language content. Equity means asking who is included and who is left out before scaling a system.

sections.heading: Privacy and change
sections.text: Privacy requires lawful purpose, consent where required, limited access, secure storage and retention rules. Data protection law differs by country, so check the current national law and institutional policy. Change management is the planned process of gaining support, training staff, piloting, reviewing and sustaining use. Leaders should explain the purpose, protect time for training, and listen to teachers. A tool succeeds only when people trust the data and use it well.

keyPoints: Digital transformation means changing work processes with technology, not just buying devices.
An EMIS collects, stores and reports education data, and its value depends on complete, timely and accurate returns.
Completeness = returns received ÷ returns expected × 100%; a share = subgroup ÷ total × 100%.
Learning analytics can flag patterns such as missed assignments, but it does not prove cause.
Equity and privacy must be designed in, because digital tools can widen exclusion and expose personal data.
Change management needs purpose, training, piloting, feedback and trust before a system is scaled.
